chapter: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
title: Critics on artists' payrolls: Feather, Gleason and Stanley Dance
summary: Hodes and DeMichael discuss critics paid by the artists they review. They cite Feather and Ellington, Gleason and Ray Charles, and Stanley Dance.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: But you said something before that these people who did it were not true people to their own beliefs. In fact, they were taking money for plugging people that they were supposed to be criticizing or writing critical analysis on.
That was just Leonard at the time. He was working as a press agent for Duke Ellington, and at the same time, he was reviewing Ellington concerts and writing about
And as a professional, I find that appalling.
And didn't you also say that, Gleason later on did it on the West Coast?
Yeah. Duke Ellington and Ray Charles. And when I found out about it, and I was at DownBeat by then, I would not let him write about those people. Because I found out that he was on their payroll.
It was unethical. Stanley Dance the same way.
This is what I thought, that there was no -- if you want to criticize -- well, this is the trouble with this. Because of Leonard, then you get a Stanley Dance coming along a little later in his camp.
Oh, I don't think Stanley is in Leonard's camp.
No, but I got a review of a record with Barney Bigard , and he just was almost crying when Barney made that record with me.
Should have been with an Ellington group or something.
Yes, yeah, he was almost crying. But I see so much throwbacks to the old.

There's still some of the old-fashioned critics, if you want to call them that, and I know them all and I consider them my friends. But it's still -- I was saying old-fashioned. But to me, it is unethical for Stanley for all those years to be on Ellington's payroll and writing about Ellington, interviewing the sidemen as he did for me in DownBeat, is one thing. But to review an Ellington record as he did in the Saturday Review, or write about a performance in nothing but glowing terms -- and now the same thing is true with Stanley and Earl Hines. He works for Earl Hines.

So I can't believe anything that Stanley writes about Earl Hines or, when Duke was alive, about Duke. Now, he's a great officiator and he doesn't see it as a conflict of interests. He sees it as -- he loves those people, he loves the music. But to me, he's still is unethical. And I love Stanley.
Yeah. If you was in government and they found that out they'd get rid of you because you've got a conflict of interest.
